title: Flag Suspicious Payments
statement:
A payments log is a list of strings shaped "name,minute,amount,city", for example "kim,10,300,seoul". The minute and amount are whole numbers.

A payment is suspicious if at least one of these is true:

  • its amount is more than 1000;
  • there is a different payment by the same name, in a different city, at most 60 minutes away (before or after, 60 included).

Return every suspicious payment string, exactly as it appears in the log. If the same string appears twice in the log and is suspicious, return it twice. Any order is accepted.

examples.why: Same name, different cities, 55 minutes apart. Both payments are flagged, not just the later one.
Only the amount rule fires. Different names never make each other suspicious.
Minute 100 and minute 161 are 61 apart, too far. Minutes 140 and 161 are in different cities 21 apart, so those two are flagged. The payment at 100 has no partner and stays clean.

constraints: name and city are 1–10 lowercase letters
hints: The amount rule looks at one payment alone. The city rule needs pairs. Which pairs can matter at all?
Only payments with the same name can make each other suspicious. Parse each string once into fields before comparing anything.

With n ≤ 1000, comparing every pair of payments is fine. For each pair with the same name, different cities and |t1 − t2| ≤ 60, mark both. Then output every marked payment and every payment over 1000.

explain.intuition:
This is mostly careful parsing and reading the rule exactly. Split each string once into name, minute, amount and city, and keep the original string to return it. A payment is flagged by its own amount, or because a partner exists. When you find a partner pair, mark both sides.

With up to 1000 payments, checking all pairs is about 500 000 comparisons, which is fast. If the log were much longer, group by name and look only at nearby minutes: store, for each name and minute, the set of cities seen there. Then a payment only has to check 121 minutes (60 on each side, plus its own), and only needs to find a city different from its own.
steps: Parse every payment into [name, minute, amount, city], keeping its index.
Create a flagged boolean per index. Set it when amount > 1000.
For every pair i < j with the same name, different cities and |minute_i − minute_j| ≤ 60, set both flags.
Return the original strings whose flag is set.
pitfalls: Flagging only the later payment of a pair. Both are suspicious, as the first example shows.
Using < 60 instead of ≤ 60, or flagging pairs in the same city.
Deduplicating the output with a set of strings. Identical log lines are separate payments and each must appear once per occurrence.

complexity.time: O(n²) for all pairs; O(n · 121) with the minute buckets

solutions.title: Compare every pair
solutions.idea: Parse once, flag big amounts, then check every pair with the same name for a different city within 60 minutes.

solutions.title: Cities by name and minute
solutions.idea: Index every payment as name → minute → set of cities. A payment needs a partner only if some minute within 60 of its own holds a city other than its own.

followups: Payments stream in sorted by minute and you must flag them as soon as possible. What do you keep in memory?
The window is no longer 60 minutes but up to a week, in seconds. Which solution survives, and what would you change?
